concept.name: Population mean
concept.definition: The mean of the entire population (or data-generating process), denoted mu; equivalently, the expected value of the underlying probability distribution. It is a fixed but typically unknown parameter that sample statistics estimate.
concept.intuition: It is the 'true average' you would get if you could observe every possible outcome - the quantity your sample mean is trying to approximate.
concept.mechanics: For a finite population of N items, mu = (1/N) SUM x_i; for a probability distribution, mu = E[X] (the probability-weighted average). Because the population is rarely fully observable, mu is estimated by the sample mean, with uncertainty quantified by the standard error and confidence intervals.
concept.formula: Finite population: mu = (1/N) * SUM_{i=1..N} x_i. Distributional: mu = E[X] = SUM x*P(x) (discrete) or integral x*f(x) dx (continuous).
concept.failure_modes: In non-stationary markets the population mean is a moving target - the 'true' mean return of one regime does not describe the next - so even a perfectly estimated historical mu has limited forward content. For distributions without a finite first moment, mu does not exist at all.
concept.misconceptions: Mu is not 'the average of a big sample'; it is a parameter of the underlying process, conceptually independent of any data. And a long sample does not guarantee the sample mean is close to a current mu when the process drifts.
concept.example: The sample mean of 10 years of daily equity returns is an estimate of mu, but the 2020 volatility regime change means the pre-2020 mu may no longer describe the current process.
